written.myAnswer: Data communication is the exchange of data between two or more devices through a transmission medium. Its components are the sender, receiver, message, transmission medium, and protocol.
Routers connect different networks and forward data packets toward their destinations using appropriate routes.
The Network Layer provides logical addressing and routing, forwarding packets between networks toward their destinations.
Packet switching divides data into packets that can travel over shared routes. Circuit switching establishes a dedicated communication path for the duration of the communication.
DHCP automatically assigns devices IP addresses and other network configuration.
Encapsulation adds protocol information, such as headers, to data to support its organisation and delivery. It does not by itself encrypt data or guarantee secure communication.
TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery and retransmits lost data when necessary. UDP has lower overhead but does not guarantee delivery or order.
Encryption converts readable data into an encoded form that unauthorised people cannot readily understand. The intended recipient can decrypt it using the appropriate key.
Star topology is relatively easy to install and manage. A failure of one device or its link usually does not affect the others, and faults are easier to locate.
Firewalls monitor and control incoming and outgoing network traffic according to security rules, helping prevent unauthorised access.
Computer networks enable resource sharing and data communication. They allow users to share hardware, software, files, and services, and to exchange messages and other data efficiently.
(a) 10 kilobits = 10,000 bits; time = 10,000 ÷ 500 = 20 seconds. (b) 10 kilobytes = 10 × 1024 × 8 = 81,920 bits; time = 81,920 ÷ 500 = 163.84 seconds.

Packet switching divides a message into packets sent over shared network routes and reassembled at the destination. Circuit switching establishes a dedicated path that remains reserved for the communication.

Protocols are agreed rules that enable devices to communicate correctly. TCP/IP supports addressing and delivery across networks; HTTP transfers web information; DNS translates domain names into IP addresses; and DHCP automatically assigns IP configuration.

Firewalls control network traffic and help block unauthorised access; encryption makes data unreadable without the appropriate key; and antivirus software detects and removes malicious software. Used together and kept updated, these methods provide complementary protection, though none is sufficient against every threat.

Businesses use networks to communicate and share files, printers, and services. Education uses them for learning platforms and sharing resources. Healthcare uses them to access patient information and support communication among healthcare staff.

In a star, each device connects to a central hub or switch; in a ring, devices form a closed loop; in a bus, devices share a backbone; and in a mesh, devices have multiple interconnections. These topologies differ in cost, reliability, and ease of troubleshooting.
